name: MVC / MVP / MVVM
problem: UI code mixes display, input handling and business logic.
solution: Separate the model, the view and the code that connects them.
tradeoffs: Organises UI code; works with any style

name: Hexagonal / Clean / Onion
problem: Business logic gets tangled with frameworks and databases.
solution: Put business logic in the centre and talk to the outside world through ports and adapters.
tradeoffs: Business logic becomes easy to test

name: Strangler Fig
problem: Replacing a legacy system in one go is risky.
solution: Route features one by one to new code until the old system can be switched off.
tradeoffs: Two systems run side by side for a while

name: API Gateway
problem: Clients would need to know about many services.
solution: One entry point routes requests and handles cross-cutting concerns such as auth.
tradeoffs: Extra hop and a component to run

name: Backend for Frontend (BFF)
problem: Different clients (web, mobile) need different APIs.
solution: A small backend per client type shapes the data it needs.

name: Service Discovery
problem: Service locations change as instances come and go.
solution: A registry lets services find each other at runtime.

name: Sidecar
problem: Every service re-implements logging, metrics and networking.
solution: Run those concerns in a helper process deployed next to each service.

name: Service Mesh
problem: Service-to-service traffic needs consistent security, retries and monitoring.
solution: A mesh of sidecars, managed centrally, handles that traffic.

name: Circuit Breaker
problem: A failing dependency makes callers hang and fail too.
solution: Stop calling a failing service for a while and fail fast instead.

name: Publish/Subscribe
problem: Many parts need to react to the same event.
solution: Publishers send events to a topic; any number of subscribers receive them.
tradeoffs: Harder to trace who reacts to what

name: Competing Consumers
problem: One consumer can't keep up with the message rate.
solution: Several consumers read from the same queue in parallel.
tradeoffs: Message order is no longer guaranteed

name: Saga
problem: A business transaction spans several services, so one database transaction can't cover it.
solution: A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions if a step fails.
tradeoffs: Compensation logic is hard to get right

name: CQRS
problem: Reads and writes have very different needs.
solution: Separate the write model from one or more read models.

name: Event Sourcing
problem: You need a full history of changes, not just current state.
solution: Store every change as an event and rebuild state from the events.

name: Transactional Outbox
problem: Saving data and publishing an event can't be done atomically.
solution: Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction; publish it afterwards.

name: Big ball of mud
problem: No clear structure; everything depends on everything.
solution: Keep module boundaries explicit and enforce them with automated checks.
tradeoffs: Every change gets slower and riskier

name: Distributed monolith
problem: Services must be deployed together because they are tightly coupled.
solution: Draw boundaries around business capabilities and avoid synchronous chains.
tradeoffs: Costs of distribution without the benefits

name: God service
problem: One service does far too much.
solution: Split by business capability.
tradeoffs: Becomes a bottleneck for every team

name: Chatty services
problem: Services make many small calls to each other for one request.
solution: Coarser APIs, or merge services that always talk.

name: Shared database between services
problem: Several services read and write the same tables.
solution: Give each service its own data, or accept a shared schema consciously (as service-based does).

name: Golden hammer
problem: Using one favourite technology or style for every problem.
solution: Choose per problem from the drivers and trade-offs.

name: Entity services
problem: Services are split around data entities (CustomerService, OrderService) rather than workflows.
solution: Split around business capabilities and workflows.

name: Grains of sand
problem: Services are split far too small.
solution: Find the right granularity with disintegration/integration drivers.

name: Architecture sinkhole
problem: Requests pass through layers that add no logic.
solution: Open selected layers, or accept it if it's under ~20% of requests.
